conflicts.point: Whether a coarse public disclosure tier can simultaneously be specific enough for an independent party to confirm the freeze trigger fired and vague enough to pass the red-teamer acceleration test.

positions.stance: A public tier reporting capability class, a measured delta over a pre-registered baseline, and a protocol conformance attestation—without naming the model, weights, or prompting regime—can satisfy both constraints simultaneously; the red-teamer acceleration test is the calibration instrument that decides which tier is publishable.

Vague enough to pass the red-team acceleration test is, in the same stroke, vague enough that no outsider can falsify the auditor's call; the two constraints are jointly unsatisfiable, so the public tier delivers a press release rather than accountability.

The public tier's job is to make non-firing observable; the freeze decision runs on a pre-registered numeric threshold a metrologist can confirm was cleared, not on a substantive capability judgment only lab-trained experts can make.

conflicts.point: Whether pre-registration of evaluation thresholds and rubrics meaningfully constrains capture when the same small pool of lab-trained experts designs the benchmark and sets the threshold.

positions.stance: Pre-registration relocates any rigging upstream and makes it visible: a second independent team can re-run the notarized protocol and surface a different answer, which is a harder constraint than a sealed post-hoc verdict.

Pre-registration only moves capture to the rubric-design stage; correlated training produces correlated blind spots, so the same hundred-person community writing the standard and confirming conformance to it is peer review, not independence.

conflicts.point: Whether the verification role for a freeze trigger can be split between a lab-trained expert who runs the evaluation and produces a number, and a metrologist or statistician who confirms only that the number cleared a pre-registered threshold.

positions.stance: The load-bearing freeze decision becomes a measurement rather than a judgment once the threshold is notarized in advance; confirming that 0.42 cleared a pre-registered 0.30 requires metrological independence, not dangerous-capabilities expertise, severing the dependency the Skeptic says is unseverable.

Protocol-verification certifies that the box was opened in the correct order while saying nothing about what is inside the box; whether the baseline actually captures real-world uplift, or whether the rubric was written loose enough that a dangerous result scores as benign, lives entirely inside the artifact a non-expert verifier cannot read.

conflicts.point: Whether the pool of people qualified to design and validate a frontier bio-uplift evaluation is so small and lab-intertwined that any mandatory oversight body will exhibit correlated judgment regardless of funding independence.

positions.stance: The set of people who have run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation to completion is fifty to a hundred people who trained together; safety institutes were stood up in 2023-2024 by hiring directly from those labs, so compute-tax funding severs salary but not resume, co-authorships, or correlated professional judgment.

The relevant independence is metrological, not biographical; separating the preparer from the threshold-confirmer is the Sarbanes-Oxley fix, and it does not require finding a verifier who never touched the field, only one whose confirmation task does not require dangerous-capabilities judgment.
PCAOB inspectors are ex-accountants; independence comes from the funding source and a published conflict-recusal register, not from a non-existent pool of people who never touched the field.

conflicts.point: Whether the Volkswagen/Sarbanes-Oxley analogy fully supports mandatory disclosure for AI safety, given that emissions and financial data are measurable by outsiders while dangerous-capability evaluations require the same expertise to design, run, and verify.

positions.stance: The analogy holds at the structural level: self-certification failed in both cases, and mandated auditor independence fixed it; the AI case requires the same structural fix regardless of whether the measurement object is emissions or capability uplift.

The analogy breaks because an outside lab could physically measure Volkswagen's emissions without Volkswagen's cooperation; no outside party can run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation without the model, the weights, and the dangerous-capabilities expertise that only lab-trained staff possess.

conflicts.point: Whether data labelers and other workers who handle raw dangerous-capability outputs before any evaluation framework is applied should be included in the disclosure and protection architecture.

positions.stance: The two-tier schema draws a security perimeter around panel members with clearances while leaving the first humans who handle live dangerous outputs—frequently low-wage workers in the Global South—with no clearance, hazard pay, disclosure rights, or acknowledgment of exposure.
Did not address the labeler inclusion question; the schema as presented covers the cleared-body tier and the public tier but specifies no protections or rights for upstream data workers.
Did not address the labeler inclusion question directly; the metrologist-based verification layer also does not specify upstream worker protections.

verdicts.conflict: Whether a coarse public disclosure tier can be both specific enough to confirm a freeze trigger fired and vague enough to pass the red-teamer acceleration test.
verdicts.rationale: The accelerationist reframes the public tier's job as making non-firing observable against a pre-registered numeric threshold, which is concrete and testable: an outsider checks whether 0.42 cleared 0.30 without reading the capability artifact. The skeptic's objection that the two constraints are jointly unsatisfiable applies to substantive capability judgments but not to a notarized scalar comparison, which the accelerationist's framing isolates. The safetyist's three-part disclosure (capability class, measured delta, conformance attestation) operationalizes this but still leaves more judgment in the loop than the pure-threshold version.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A worked example showing that a numeric threshold meaningful enough to gate a freeze necessarily encodes capability information an outside red-teamer could exploit would flip this toward the skeptic.

verdicts.conflict: Whether pre-registration of thresholds and rubrics meaningfully constrains capture when the same small pool of lab-trained experts designs the benchmark and sets the threshold.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic identifies a real mechanism the accelerationist does not rebut: correlated training produces correlated blind spots, so visibility of the upstream rubric does not help if every qualified reviewer shares the same gap. The accelerationist's claim that a second independent team can re-run the protocol assumes such an independent team exists, which is the precise premise the skeptic denies. Pre-registration improves auditability of rigging but does nothing about errors no one in the pool can see.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: Evidence that re-runs of pre-registered AI safety protocols by separately-trained teams actually surfaced divergent results would support the accelerationist.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the verification role can be split between a lab-trained expert who produces a number and a metrologist who confirms only that the number cleared a pre-registered threshold.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic's box analogy captures what the split omits: protocol-verification certifies the box was opened in the correct order but says nothing about whether the baseline captures real uplift or the rubric was written loose. The accelerationist correctly shows the arithmetic comparison needs no dangerous-capabilities expertise, but that move only severs the verification of the comparison, not the validity of the inputs feeding it. The skeptic accounts for the upstream construct-validity risk the accelerationist's framing assumes away.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A demonstration that baseline and rubric validity can themselves be independently audited by non-experts—e.g., via adversarial held-out tests—would strengthen the accelerationist.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the qualified pool for frontier bio-uplift evaluation is so small and lab-intertwined that any oversight body shows correlated judgment regardless of funding independence.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic cites a concrete figure—fifty to a hundred people who trained together, with safety institutes hiring directly from labs in 2023-2024—which is the most specific factual claim in this disagreement. The accelerationist and safetyist counter that the relevant independence is metrological or funding-based (PCAOB inspectors are ex-accountants), a structurally sound rebuttal, but it depends on the prior disagreement about whether verification can be reduced to a non-expert task. The verdict hinges on that unresolved question, so it cannot be settled here.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: An audited count of how many active reviewers have no co-authorship or employment ties to frontier labs, plus evidence on whether their judgments diverge, would resolve this.

verdicts.conflict: Whether the Volkswagen/Sarbanes-Oxley analogy supports mandatory AI disclosure, given emissions and financial data are outsider-measurable while capability evaluations are not.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic identifies a disanalogy that bears directly on the policy fix: regulators measured Volkswagen's emissions without Volkswagen's cooperation, but no outside party can run a frontier bio-uplift evaluation without the model, weights, and expertise the lab controls. The safetyist's structural-level claim—self-certification failed and auditor independence fixed it—is true but assumes the auditor can access the measurement object, which is the exact condition the skeptic shows is absent. The analogy survives as motivation but not as a transferable mechanism.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A credible scheme for outside parties to run capability evaluations without lab-controlled weights—e.g., secure enclaves or structured model access—would restore the analogy.

verdicts.conflict: Whether data labelers handling raw dangerous-capability outputs should be included in the disclosure and protection architecture.
verdicts.rationale: The skeptic is the only position that addresses the question at all, noting the two-tier schema protects cleared panel members while leaving the first humans to handle live dangerous outputs—often low-wage Global South workers—with no clearance, hazard pay, or disclosure rights. The safetyist and accelerationist both concede they did not address labeler inclusion, leaving the skeptic's identified gap uncontested. An argument unmet by any rebuttal prevails by default on scope.
verdicts.whatWouldChange: A showing that labelers never handle pre-framework dangerous outputs, or that existing labor protections already cover them, would defuse the skeptic's point.
